cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the feeling you have for this person is your own.
cells.ask: Name one thing you feel about someone you're close to and say it to them this week, plainly, without adding what you want back.
cells.core:
You can feel what someone else is feeling and still know where you stop. That's not a small thing — most people either lose themselves in the other person or hold them at arm's length. You're doing neither. You're in the room, you're taking them in, and you're still the one standing there.

The feeling you have for people is real and it's yours to hand over. When you stay that close to someone without dissolving into them, you're building something that will outlast this stretch — a way of being with people that doesn't cost you yourself. The straightforward move is to say what you feel, once, to someone who'll receive it. Keep going.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel with someone and still be your own.

cells.tense: You are already feeling what others haven't said, bracing for a weight that hasn't been handed to you.
cells.ask: Pick one person you're carrying in your head and put them down for a day — no checking, no pre-solving, no rehearsing what they'll need.
cells.core:
You feel so far into other people that their feeling and yours arrive as one thing. Someone walks in and you're already carrying what they haven't said yet. It feels like love, and some of it is — but you're also living ahead of them, in a future where their problem has already become yours. That's a lot of weight, and much of it hasn't actually been handed to you.

There's a line between feeling with someone and disappearing into them. You've been standing on the far side of it. The cost is that you're not here with the person in front of you; you're ahead of them, braced. Pulling back isn't feeling less. It's letting one worry stay theirs, and finding out that they carry it fine. Staying close to someone doesn't require carrying them.
cells.sheetLine: You feel so far into people that you end up ahead of them.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed a long time ago, and your hands aren't reaching for anyone.
cells.ask: Ask one person one real question about their life and stay in the answer for two minutes without planning what to say next.
cells.core:
You can be in a room with someone for an hour and come out with nothing of them. Not because you don't care — asking and listening are the two moves that build the feeling, and both of them have gone quiet. Now everything stays on the surface, and the surface is flat.

The room where this works is a small one. You ask something real, and you listen to the whole answer without deciding what's next. What they say lands in you and changes what you say back. That exchange is the mechanism — a live adjustment, made as you go. Begin with one question and stay in it. You don't have to feel anything big. Just be there for the answer and let it move you a little.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped letting anyone in, and it shows.

cells.tense: You are already feeling with people, and you call it something else — practicality, or just getting through the day.
cells.ask: Tell one person why you did something for them, and use a word for the feeling instead of the reason you'd normally give.
cells.core:
People around you can feel that you're with them — it's in how you show up, what you notice, what you do without being asked. But if someone asked you whether you care, you'd say you were just being practical. The feeling is running the whole time. You're just not claiming it.

That's the gap. The connection is real and it's doing work, and you're the only one who doesn't see it as yours. You keep describing what you do for people as logistics, as habit, as just how you are. The same care, seen as care, is a different life. Next time you do something for someone, say the feeling instead of the reason.
cells.sheetLine: You're already feeling with people. You just don't call it that.

A reader could fairly say the reading is wrong about them entirely, so the ask must be useful even if the diagnosis misses — it is a small, observable act around one person, not a mood fix. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line that sounds like a verdict on who they are; I've cut that and left only what they can answer back to.
